analysis.summary: The critical path is a serial multiply-accumulate with saturation: b1_q feeds a multiplier to produce p1, which enters a three-stage ripple adder chain (s0 + p1 → s1 + p2 → s2 + p3), followed by a wide 40-bit comparison and ternary mux to select the saturated output. The serial accumulation chain with ripple carry dominates the delay, followed by the end-of-path saturation logic that must wait for all accumulation to complete.

bottlenecks.pattern: serial accumulate chain with ripple carry
bottlenecks.root_cause: Three 40-bit additions are sequenced serially (s1 = s0 + p1; s2 = s1 + p2; s3 = s2 + p3), each depending on the result of the previous. Each addition implements carry ripple propagation, requiring ~40 logic levels per add.
bottlenecks.evidence: 86 combinational cells in path, 52 AOI/OAI cells (carry chain indicators), 12 XOR cells (sum bits); 87 stages in endpoint region contributing 2.0487 ns

bottlenecks.pattern: wide comparison with ternary mux at path end
bottlenecks.root_cause: 40-bit greater-than and less-than comparisons (s3 > LIMIT; s3 < -LIMIT) complete only after the full accumulation chain. The ternary mux selecting sat_val must then wait for these comparison results, serializing the comparison logic into the critical path.
bottlenecks.evidence: 12 OR3_X1 cells and additional AOI21 cells for wide comparison and mux tree; comparison logic embedded in the 87-stage endpoint region (mac_chain.v:81)

bottlenecks.root_cause: The b1_q input register output fans out heavily (fanout 42) to the 16-bit multiplier and downstream accumulator stages. High fanout increases transition time and degrades stage delay on this critical signal.

candidates.directive: Attack bottleneck #2 (or the next-ranked one if #2 is minor). Leave bottleneck #1 alone entirely, so that the group can tell the two fixes apart.
candidates.pattern: wide comparison at end of datapath
candidates.strategy: replace full comparators with high-bit saturation detection
candidates.rationale: A 40-bit comparator adds ~20 logic levels after the accumulation chain completes. For LIMIT = 2^37-1, saturation is decided by the top 3 bits (sign and two magnitude bits) — checking these directly via 2-3 gates instead of full magnitude comparison recovers ~200ps of critical-path delay. Synthesis will flatten the bit checks into lower fanout gates than ripple comparison.
candidates.area_cost: none, logic is simpler than the original comparators
candidates.equivalence_argument: The saturation conditions are mathematically identical at all representable values. For s3 > LIMIT (2^37-1): iff s3 is positive AND contains a 1 in positions [38:37]. For s3 < -LIMIT (-(2^37-1)): iff s3 is negative AND is not in the narrow range [-2^37+1, -1] that keeps bits [38:37]=11. The ternary mux then selects the same output in both implementations, bit for bit, regardless of input.

abstracted.evidence: cand0 & cand3 both scored -0.4789 (A_i -0.7460, best in group), WNS -0.1620 ns, identical area. These candidates are equivalent transformations, proving consistency of the approach.

cand1 scored -0.3682 (A_i -0.1958). While ~0.5 units behind pure rebalancing, it achieved better WNS (-0.2138 ns) and remained area-neutral (+28um² vs baseline), offering a viable alternative when tree rebalancing is unavailable.

cand2 scored 0.0105 (A_i +1.6878, worst in group). WNS degraded to -0.3606 ns and TNS worsened to -3.8075 ns (vs. -1.5467 ns baseline). The high-bit shortcut ignored the true bottleneck: the upstream accumulation chain itself. This strategy only helps if the comparator is the critical path, not the source.

skill_learning.observations: The group reveals a clear hierarchy: binary-tree rebalancing of the accumulation chain is the dominant fix (cand0/3 tied for best), parallelizing saturation provides a weaker but viable alternative (cand1), and attacking the wrong bottleneck with a clever optimization (cand2) actively hurts. The equivalence of cand0 and cand3—identical metrics despite different phrasing—confirms that the rebalancing principle is robust and synthesis-independent. The saturation-parallelization approach is instructive: it does help (cand1 beats baseline in WNS), but not as much as solving the arithmetic bottleneck first.
